title: What was the original "blockbuster"? | MOVIE WORDS

entries.note: Named for things that move: a shortening of [[from:moving pictures]], barely a century old; in England saying it sounds slightly pretentious compared with [[see:film]].
Jess understood early that it came from talking pictures, long before realising [[see:movie]] works the same way.
A phrase from about the same time as moving pictures, the source of [[see:movie]].
The usual British word, as old as English itself: Old English [[from:filmen]] meant a membrane or tissue, and specifically the foreskin.
A spin-off of [[from:photography]], meaning drawing with movement.
Literally drawing with light, from its Greek elements; the model for [[gave:cinematography]].
A more Greek-looking early alternative to cinema, spelled with a K and as common as cinema in the early days; related to German [[same-root:Kino]].
The German word for cinema, linked to the early English form [[same-root:kinema]].
A Greek–Latin hybrid meaning far seer, used around 1900 before the device existed; [[see:John Logie Baird]] called his machine the [[see:televisor]].
Credited with the first live [[see:television]] broadcast in the mid-1920s, building on others' work.
[[see:John Logie Baird]]'s name for his machine; [[see:television]] caught on instead.
One of the other proposed names for [[see:television]]-like technology before it existed.
Another early proposed name for [[see:television]]; Vista still appears in many film and TV terms and brands.
Now a pay TV channel; originally a theatre showing films for a nickel, plus a Greek element for a roofed theatre, as in [[see:Odeon]].
Still a British cinema brand; the nickelodeons were modelled on a Paris music hall called the Odéon.
Name of dime museums and a Boston music hall, cited alongside [[see:nickelodeon]].
One of several old words for movies that didn't catch on.
An old word for movies; Jess reckons its coiner was proud of it and annoyed it never caught on.
One of the old, unsuccessful words for movies.
One of the old, unsuccessful words for movies.
An old word for movies that really caught on in South Africa, though it is now somewhat antiquated.
Rob's grandma went to the flicks; flick is still heard and survives in [[see:Netflix]].
Its name preserves the old word [[see:flicks]].
A cute old way of saying motion picture, spelled like a glass jug.
Named after heavy paper for preliminary sketches; popularised for editorial drawings by [[see:Punch]], applied to animation around 1916 through [[see:Winsor McCay]].
Probably popularised [[see:cartoon]] for editorial drawings.
One possible starting point for animation, which became the [[see:cartoon]].
A little pinhole camera, the other possible starting point for animation.
Animation pioneer and newspaper cartoonist who led people to call early animated films [[see:cartoon]]s; made [[see:Little Nemo]] and [[see:Gertie the Dinosaur]].
[[see:Winsor McCay]]'s 1911 animated film.
[[see:Winsor McCay]]'s 1914 animated film, which can still be watched.
The spinning device usually showing a galloping horse; its name also derives from a word meaning movement.
A British WWII bomb that shattered a city block, used hyperbolically from 1942 for a smash; first applied to the film [[see:Bombardier]], probably as a deliberate pun.
The first film called a [[see:blockbuster]], likely a deliberate pun on the bomb.
American term for touring actors performing in barns, then a second-rate actor, then touring politicians, musicians, sports teams and display pilots; also a Disney World coaster.
Meaning music plus action, from Greek elements, like [[see:melody]] and [[see:drama]]; existing since the 1700s and common in early silent films.
Victorian theatre slang first for an actor playing a corpse breaking character, then anyone breaking character; now narrowed to laughing.
Also from theatre: the fourth wall is the imaginary barrier hiding the audience; a more intentional version of [[see:corpsing]].
Used by Shakespeare for a respected senior person, one step below master; then a foreman, the lead set electrician, and a football manager; Samwise Gamgee's father is the Gaffer.
A crew member who takes instructions from the [[see:gaffer]].
Takes instructions from the [[see:gaffer]]; it has also meant a stage hand since the 1800s.
The person who operates the [[see:dolly]] used for tracking shots.
A railroad-style cart for tracking shots; all dollies go back to devices with limbs like a child's doll, beginning with the [[from:dumb dolly]].
The [[see:gaffer]]'s assistant, especially in electrics; perhaps from a term for a favoured apprentice, fixed by early call sheets and used regardless of gender.
A really important role, unlike the British TV [[see:runner]].
In a British TV studio, the person who fetches the cups of tea, unlike a [[see:showrunner]].
A shot moving on a track, related through [[see:dolly]] to the [[same-root:Barbie doll]].
An 18th-century washing device with wooden legs and two arms, the first [[gave:dolly]].
An example of a [[see:dolly]] named for a round head-like part.
Related to the film [[same-root:dolly shot]].
Someone working for Craft Services, the on-set food service for cast and crew, the people responsible for film craft.
A grip cart loaded with flags, stands and apple boxes, jokingly named for resembling a metal taco holder; not for food.
A stencil placed in front of a light to cast shapes; possibly from goes before optics, though that may be reverse engineering.
Not a backronym for wind, reel and print, since printing happens daily; probably just from wrapping up.
The long microphone pole, named after a sailboat's nautical boom, which might also whack you in the face.
A deliberate distraction in politics; on set a furry microphone cover, called dead because it mutes wind and looks lifeless; once more commonly a [[equivalent:wind sock]].
Another name for the furry microphone cover, the [[equivalent:dead cat]].
The older, more common name for the [[equivalent:dead cat]], avoiding images of a fallen feline.
Filming without sound, supposedly from a German director saying mit out sound; possibly just a recurring industry gag about 1920s German directors.
A name for westerns made by Italians, compared with the joke behind [[see:MOS]].
The Directors Guild's sanctioned pseudonym for disowning directors, from [[see:Death of a Gunfighter]]; [[see:Al Smith]] was rejected as too common.
1969 film where an actor got the director sacked; neither director wanted credit, leading to [[gave:Alan Smithee]].
The first fake name considered, rejected as too common, before [[see:Alan Smithee]].
David Lynch disowned an edited cut, crediting [[see:Alan Smithee]] instead, after putting his name on the theatrical release.
The American documentarian's slow zoom or pan across a still image, now named after him in the audiovisual industry.
Sound effects made by recording something else, like snapping a carrot for bones; named after [[from:Jack Foley]].
Silent-era Hollywood sound designer said to make movies sound better than real life; [[gave:Foley]] is named after him.
Sound that exists within the story world, like character dialogue, as opposed to [[see:non-diegetic]] sound.
Sound external to the narrative, like voiceovers and the score, as opposed to [[see:diegetic]] sound.
Supposedly popularised by [[see:Seinfeld]]; sounds Yiddish but isn't, with versions from 1825 apparently from a northern English dialect.
Supposedly popularised [[see:yada yada yada]].
Industry term for background noise or chatter, from extras saying [[see:walla walla]].
What extras were told to say to sound like they were talking, without distracting words; also a Washington place name.
The other famous filler extras mutter, as on EastEnders; an [[equivalent:walla walla]].
What Jess was told to say as a theatre kid; Rob thinks it looks more like English speech than [[equivalent:rhubarb rhubarb rhubarb]].
Another background filler phrase like [[equivalent:watermelon]].
Another suggested background filler phrase that might actually work.
An ultimately unimportant plot device, loved by [[see:Alfred Hitchcock]], probably coined by [[see:Angus MacPhail]], whose name may have shaped it; guff means nonsense.
Loved using the [[see:MacGuffin]].
Screenwriter who probably coined [[see:MacGuffin]], his name perhaps shaping it.
A verb for improvising a fix, from the TV character who made tools from gum and duct tape; British English says [[equivalent:bodging]].
The British word for improvising a fix, equivalent to [[equivalent:MacGyver]].
Popularised words including [[see:cromulent]] and [[see:embiggen]].
A joke nonword from The Simpsons, now used unironically and in dictionaries; Rob links his dislike of [[see:winningest]] to it.
Simpsons nonsense word for acceptable; Latin [[from:-ulentus]], full of, as in [[see:flatulent]]; Jess half-jokingly links crom to a Welsh root meaning crooked.
Rob dislikes it, seen of a jockey in NPR, sounding like [[see:embiggen]]; Jess grew up hearing it of [[see:Pat Summitt]].
Tennessee Lady Vols coach, one of the [[see:winningest]] coaches ever; a new WNBA team, the Summit, nods to her.
An example of the Latin ending meaning full of, also seen in [[see:cromulent]].
From Happy Days, where Fonzie jumps a shark in the first of many bad episodes; it means a show's sharp downturn in quality.
A character introduced just to die, from [[see:Star Trek]]'s doomed red-shirted crew; shows nod to it with red shirts.
Where red-shirted crew tended to die, giving [[gave:red shirt]].
Using a false online identity to deceive someone into a relationship, from the TV show [[from:Catfish]].
TV show about unmet online couples, titled from an apocryphal anecdote about a catfish kept with live cod to keep them active.
Unrecorded before 2006 despite older [[see:kick the bucket]]; even the OED traces it to the film The Bucket List, though people insist otherwise, a [[see:Mandela effect]].
A much older phrase, which makes people think [[see:bucket list]] predates the film.
A collective misremembering, used to describe beliefs about [[see:bucket list]].
You're toast is first found in [[see:Ghostbusters]], where [[see:Bill Murray]] ad-libbed this chick is toast; earlier idioms like [[see:served on toast]] date to the 1800s.
An 1800s idiom about beating someone, predating [[see:toast]] in the we're-toast sense.
The film where the you're-[[see:toast]] construction is first found.
Ad-libbed this chick is toast in [[see:Ghostbusters]], from the scripted turn this guy into toast.
One of several movie-derived terms now used generally.
A movie-derived term that, with [[see:blue pill]], has gone off on its own horrible adventure.
A movie-derived term that, with [[see:red pill]], has gone off on its own horrible adventure.
A rebracketing from the film Inception, used for nested things or [[see:recursion]], though [[see:inception]] really means a beginning.
The real word for nesting: in linguistics, embedding structures within others, as in Rob thinks Jess is silly, potentially without end.
Actually means a beginning, so the [[see:-ception]] usage doesn't fit its meaning.
An on-screen caption graphic, also a [[equivalent:lower third]], named after the Chiron Corporation; in Britain called an [[equivalent:Aston]].
Another name for a [[equivalent:Chiron]].
British name for a [[equivalent:Chiron]], after the supplier Aston Broadcast Systems.
Named after its inventor company Teleprompter; Britain says [[equivalent:Autocue]] after the BBC's supplier; originally a paper roll above the camera, now angled glass.
The British name for a [[equivalent:teleprompter]], after the company Autocue that supplied the BBC.
To tell someone in television to start; allegedly from Latin [[from?:quando]], when; similar to [[see:prompt]].
Compared with [[see:cue]]: to prompt is to tell someone to do something.
